utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good afternoon. We're ready, I believe, for the next witness, Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, we're ready for the next witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: If the witness could be brought in.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And of course, this witness has protective measures.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes. While that is happening, at an earlier point when Mr. Guy-Smith's client was unwell, he expressed his concern that there might be reason for some further assessment of his health. The Chamber has received through the registrar a report on the present condition of Mr. Guy-Smith's client, which indicates both something of the nature of the cause of the difficulty that did interrupt the proceedings and gives a brief but pretty clear assessment of his present health and indicates the nature of regular checking and assessment that is occurring. And in view of those -- that report and what is said there, the Chamber sees no present reason for it to take any steps in respect of your client's health. Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I appreciate the Chamber's thoughts in that regard. I continue to have a concern because at one point at a prior time there was a question as to whether or not there may be some other organic difficulty going on with Mr. Bala. However, in the absence of the medical records, I'm not in a position to press the point any further. And at this point I'll have a conversation with my client and see how best to proceed in that regard. Because I am concerned that if there are any other incidents they're dealt with, with full medical understanding. But I appreciate the Chamber's position at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Guy-Smith. And so that the record is clear, we would have a copy of that report marked as an exhibit in the trial when the computer system is functioning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir. If you please read aloud the affirmation on the card what is offered to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly swear that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Examined by Mr. Whiting:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Witness. Can you hear me clearly?

utterances.speaker: Witness L-64
utterances.text: Yes, I hear you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, I want to remind you that you have been granted protective measures, which means that your image will not shown on the television and your name will not be used in these proceedings and your voice will also be distorted. Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: Witness L-64
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Also, when we talk about matters that may identify you or identify other names, we will go into private session and I will tell you when we are going into private session and ask for the Court's permission to do that. Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: Witness L-64
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'll also going to ask you to sit forward a little bit and speak into the microphone. You don't need to speak right up against the microphone but... I'm also going to ask you to take your time in answering my questions and give the interpreters time to interpret my questions and interpret your answers. Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: Witness L-64
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And if you don't understand any of my questions, just please tell me and I will rephrase it. Do you understand?

utterances.speaker: Witness L-64
utterances.text: Yes, I understand.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, I'm going to -- with the assistance of the usher show you a piece of paper. I'm going to ask you to look at the paper and tell us if that is your name on the paper.

utterances.speaker: Witness L-64
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I do see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And if that paper can be shown to the Defence counsel and to the Judge, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: While that is happening, I think the computer system is now functioning. We'll get that exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The exhibit number will be DB3.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. That is the medical report.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And if that sheet could be given a number and placed under seal, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This sheet will be marked P165 and it is under seal.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, I will refer to you today either simply as witness or by your number which is L-64. Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: Witness L-64
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, could we go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Private.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, drawing your attention to 1994, 1995, 1996, did you have any trouble with the Serb authorities?

utterances.speaker: Witness L-64
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened?

utterances.speaker: Witness L-64
utterances.text: The Serbs carried out frequent searches for arms in my home. I think it was January 1994 when the police took me and my brother. They detained us for two days at the police station. They maltreated us. They broke three of my ribs, and then they sent me out in the street to die, thinking that I would die, but then I recovered.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I want to remind you, Witness, not to say your brother's name when we're in public session. Did something happen after -- afterwards? Were you at some point arrested?

utterances.speaker: Witness L-64
utterances.text: Yes, in 1995, in May, during a routine search in my car the police found a pistol, Magnum type and I was arrested again and the criminal municipal court sentenced me to three months of prison for this offence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you serve time in prison?

utterances.speaker: Witness L-64
utterances.text: Yes. On November the 1st, 1996 I began my prison term and I was released seven or eight days before -- or ten days before the new year.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, in 1998 and 1999 were you a member of the KLA?

utterances.speaker: Witness L-64
utterances.text: Yes. As of May 1998 -- 1998, excuse me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the months of May, June and July of 1998, where did you serve in the KLA?

utterances.speaker: Witness L-64
utterances.text: In Lapusnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, moving forward in time, on the 27th of May, 2003, were you summonsed for an interview with the Office of the Prosecutor of the ICTY?

utterances.speaker: Witness L-64
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I was summonsed as a suspect of war crimes, 1998, 1999.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you arrived for the interview, was your status as a suspect or a witness addressed before the interview started?

utterances.speaker: Witness L-64
utterances.text: Yes. I can't tell how that lasted. I think it was maybe one or two hours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, my question is: Before the interview began on the 27th of May, 2003, was there a discussion about whether you were in fact considered a suspect or a witness?

utterances.speaker: Witness L-64
utterances.text: No. I said before the interview started, we had a talk which lasted I can't tell you how long, during which it was explained that I was no longer treated as a suspect but simply was there as a witness for an interview.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was that the only matter that was discussed before the recorded interview began?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Objection, leading.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: I'm sorry to rise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Mansfield.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: The problem is that as far as I'm aware we don't have any material on this. At least, I don't anyway. And this is extremely important. If there is a record again of this part of the proceedings that took place then, then we certainly should be provided with it. May I ask for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't believe there is any record. This is a minor misunderstanding which occurred before the interview and which was cleared up and is clear on the -- on the interview, that he is -- the interviewed as a witness ant not a suspect. And I just simply wanted to the clear this up before -- but it goes no further than that. And there's no --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That's the extent of evidence of this nature that you're leading.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Well now, you will rephrase your question and we will move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Yes, I didn't appreciate it would be a point of controversy which is why I thought I could lead him through it. But I will rephrase the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith tries to get us every now and then to get us back onto straight and narrow rails. It's appreciated, Mr. Guy-Smith. I hope your stamina lasted during the trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'm' doing my best. I'm doing my best.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness before the recorded interview with the Office of the Prosecutor began on the 27th of May, 2003, you've told us that -- you have already told us that were informed that you were being interviewed as a witness and not a suspect. Was any other matter discussed before the recorded interview began?

utterances.speaker: Witness L-64
utterances.text: No, I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And at the beginning of the recorded interview, is it -- do you recall whether it stated that you were being interviewed as a witness?

utterances.speaker: Witness L-64
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the 17th and 18th of June, 2003 were you again interviewed by the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: Witness L-64
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were those interviews recorded?

utterances.speaker: Witness L-64
utterances.text: Yes, they were recorded.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In addition to those interviews on those dates, did you take a trip to Lapusnik with the investigators?

utterances.speaker: Witness L-64
utterances.text: Yes, once. I can't remember when, but yes, we did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the 17th and 18th of June, did you also have discussions with the investigators that were not recorded?

utterances.speaker: Witness L-64
utterances.text: Yes, I think so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know if the matters that were discussed that were not recorded were later included in your ICTY statement which you did later?

utterances.speaker: Witness L-64
utterances.text: Yes, I have seen them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your interviews, your interview on the 27th of May 2003 and on the 17th and 18th of June, 2003, did you talk about your time in Lapusnik from May to July 1998?

utterances.speaker: Witness L-64
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could we go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Private.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in public session.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, I remind you that we are in public session so please take care not to mention your name or anything that might identify you. Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: Witness L-64
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, at the time of the arrest that we just talked about in private session, were you addicted to heroin?

utterances.speaker: Witness L-64
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Had you been addicted to heroin in the past?

utterances.speaker: Witness L-64
utterances.text: Yes, part -- during part of 2002 for some months.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did your addiction to heroin stop?

utterances.speaker: Witness L-64
utterances.text: It was a long time before the new year of 2002. I asked for the medical assistance and I underwent therapy as a doctor advised me which cost me a lot of money. But that happened before the new year.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When is the last time that you used heroin?

utterances.speaker: Witness L-64
utterances.text: Since that time before the new year, I don't remember very well. It might have been once or twice, small quantities, but I went to the doctor again and consulted him. So it was from before the new year up to February, probably, of the next year.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So is it your testimony that February of 2003 is the last time you think you used heroin?

utterances.speaker: Witness L-64
utterances.text: Either January or February. What I know is that I took two times heroin from the moment that I gave it up that I stopped. That is, from December 2002 up to January or February of 2002 -- it was once or twice.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, were you ever involved in any way in the sale of heroin?

utterances.speaker: Witness L-64
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When I ask you that I mean directly or indirectly.

utterances.speaker: Witness L-64
utterances.text: Yes, now it's clear to me. Indirectly up until the time I was a user, I might have been involved two or three times, but dealing with limited quantities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say "indirectly" what was your role in these occasions when you sold -- let me rephrase the question. When you say indirectly what was your role in these sales of heroin?

utterances.speaker: Witness L-64
utterances.text: I knew the people who were dealing with heroin and in the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. meantime I found out the persons who were interested to buy some quantities and the person could have -- could afford to buy it. So I was kind of intermediary.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And would you get some money when you acted as an intermediary?

utterances.speaker: Witness L-64
utterances.text: In one instance, yes. I got either 500 or 1,000 Deutschemarks. It's not that I asked for it, the person gave me the money to me of his own free will.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, how many times in all would you say that you acted in the this capacity as an intermediary?

utterances.speaker: Witness L-64
utterances.text: Two or three times, I think.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And during the war in 1998/1999 did you engage in this activity, act as an intermediary?

utterances.speaker: Witness L-64
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When after the war were you engaged in this activity?

utterances.speaker: Witness L-64
utterances.text: I said during this period, 2002. I don't remember the time, the date, but it was in 2002 until I was dependant on it for some time. I rather not speak about that, but it's part of my life which I can't help mentioning, even if I don't like to speak about it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'll just ask you one more question about it -- sorry, I'm going to ask you two more questions about it, and I understand that you don't like to speak about it. Can you tell us the last time that you were involved as an intermediary in a sale of heroin?

utterances.speaker: Witness L-64
utterances.text: I don't remember accurately. It was a question of a few grammes of heroin. It might have been the new year -- near the new year of 2002, but I'm not very sure about the time because at that time I used to run away from everyone I knew or when I knew that the person possessed heroin or used heroin. I did my best not to have any contacts with such individuals.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was this the time that you were trying to end your own addiction to heroin?

utterances.speaker: Witness L-64
utterances.text: Yes, yes. That was a time when I was trying to run away from everybody, even from my family and I lived alone in a village. I didn't want to have any contacts with anyone.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, can you tell us, please, the largest amount of heroin that you were involved in as an intermediary, in the sale as an intermediary?

utterances.speaker: Witness L-64
utterances.text: It's largest amount of heroin was about half a kilogramme packaged in a box, but that was not the entire amount in that box. So I can't tell you for sure whether it was more or less than half a kilogramme and zero, that is. Maybe 200 or 300 grammes but the package could get -- could hold up to half a kilogramme.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I know that you can't remember very accurately the last time that you were involved in a transaction as an intermediary, but you testified earlier that in -- it was in February of 2003 that you ended your -- you ended your addiction to heroin. After that date were you involved any heroin transactions as an intermediary?

utterances.speaker: Witness L-64
utterances.text: I think I pointed out that I stopped my addiction in 2002. But I also used once or twice again once in 2003. I'm not sure whether it was January or February. It was a small amount that I used. And after that I had nothing to do with this kind of affair, never.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, can you tell us today how you look back on this time when you were involved with heroin?

utterances.speaker: Witness L-64
utterances.text: I said that I had no idea about it. When I heard people saying that you can be become dependant on it, I didn't believe it. And I thought you can try it and you can just forget about it. But that was not the case. And when it happened to me, then I realised how hard that was and now as I said I don't like even to talk about it. Or even to hear something about that, about drug addiction. I don't like to talk about that part of my life. But when it's -- when it involves a certain reality then I have to talk about it because some of my children are very young and they don't know about that thing happening in my life, that's true. I'm very ashamed of it, but this is how it was. I hate myself for doing it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, I'll move on. After you were arrested in July of 2003, were you held in gaol?

utterances.speaker: Witness L-64
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After three months in jail did the Office of the Prosecutor of the ICTY and the international prosecutor in Kosovo to have an application to the court to have you declared a cooperative witness under the law in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: Witness L-64
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was an order issued by international judge in Pristina declaring you to be a cooperative witness?

utterances.speaker: Witness L-64
utterances.text: Yes. I think I read and signed that order.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us today in your own words what you understand that order to say?

utterances.speaker: Witness L-64
utterances.text: I thought that I wouldn't be held responsible to -- before a court for the things that I was accused of. This is how I understood it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what did the order require you to do, if anything?

utterances.speaker: Witness L-64
utterances.text: The order was that I become as a witness for -- in relation to the two interviews made earlier.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: With the assistance of the usher I'm going to put the order in front of you and draw your attention to certain parts.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: It's -- in the bundle that has been provided to the Court it's number 11.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: We have a copy here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, do you have the English? There's an Albanian version which follows the English. Could you look at the Albanian version, please. Do you have the Albanian version in front of you now?

utterances.speaker: Witness L-64
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I could draw your attention to the first paragraph on the first page. You see that you're declared a cooperative witness?

utterances.speaker: Witness L-64
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And before I continue, just to be clear, this order has been read to you in Albanian; is that right?

utterances.speaker: Witness L-64
utterances.text: Yes. It was read it me in Albanian and I think I have signed it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In paragraph 2, do you see that it states as you testified that the criminal proceedings pending against you will not continue. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: Witness L-64
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I could ask you to turn to paragraph 4. Do you see that the order requires you to testify truthfully, to give the complete truth without omission, concerning what you regarded while serving as a soldier of the KLA in Lapusnik during the summer of 1998 and in particular with respect to allegations in this case. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: Witness L-64
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Turning to paragraph 5. Do you see that in the event it is found that you testified falsely or omitted any part of the truth that the charges were pending against you could be reinstated? Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: Witness L-64
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Finally, in paragraph 6, do you see that the order does not apply to any subsequent acts committed after the time -- the time of this order and does not apply to any offence that is punishable by more than ten years of imprisonment? Do you see that in paragraph 6?

utterances.speaker: Witness L-64
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd ask that this -- this order be given an exhibit number and placed under seal. And I would also ask just for a matter of completeness that the application which led to this order which is attached at tab 10 also be exhibited and placed under seal. And I would just for purposes of the record draw the Court's attention to what I believe is a typographical error in the order. At page 4, paragraph 1, under the "because" it's -- it makes reference to the witness's prior interviews with the ICTY and it says -- and then sentence says: "At that time he was arrested or in custody on this indicted case." I believe it should be clear from the context and also from the application that it should read: "He was not arrested or in custody on this indicted case," since there is no dispute that he wasn't arrested until after the interviews on the 13th of July, 2003.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Both the order and the application will be received separately as exhibits.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The first order is P166; under seal. And the second document is P167. Is that under seal also?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Yes, that should be under seal.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The application, did you want the supporting document as well?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I think it could go in just as one number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: One number, very well. One is the application; the other is a declaration of factual allegations. Both are dated 16th of October. Together they will form the Exhibit P167.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: With regard to the representations made by Mr. Whiting concerning this official document, and specifically his interpretation of paragraph 1, I have some concerns. This is a document that was signed by international judge at the Pristina District Court. Clearly, if there are any records of those hearings and what transpired during those hearings and what the understandings were concerning the status of this gentleman, that is a matter that was dealt with then. To change the evidentiary statements made in such a document, I believe, is inappropriate in the absence of somebody coming to testify with regard it this issue or some declaration being submitted to the Court that establishes the incorrectness of the assertions that are made in the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it your position, Mr. Whiting, that in the application or the supporting document the contrary is stated? Is that what I understand from what you said, or were you relying simply on the evidence that this witness has given a moment ago?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I believe -- if I could just have a moment, Your Honour. Yes, Your Honour, it's paragraph 24 of the second document, that is, the factual declaration. And it says in reference to the witness that he gave to the ICTY OTP his statement before he was arrested. In addition, in -- in both documents it is set out the dates of his interviews with the OTP and the date of his arrest. And so I think that the -- the only logical reading of the sentence is to -- is to -- is that there is a typographical error and I think --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think, Mr. Whiting, rather than argument what you have is an order of the court which recites one statement of fact. You have the supporting materials upon which that order was made which seem to recite the contrary, you have the evidence of this witness which is to the contrary of what is recited in the order. There is therefore potentially a factual issue for decision on the basis of those various documents. I don't think your interpretation will help the resolution of that. The materials are as they are presently before us and the evidence as it is presently before us and if it becomes an issue, in the absence of anything further being placed before us, there will be a factual issue for resolution.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I appreciate that. And I will -- I will consider further whether additional evidence could be brought to bear on this particular issue. May I continue? Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, after the order was issued that we have just been discussing, were you released from prison?

utterances.speaker: Witness L-64
utterances.text: Yes. The day that I was in -- I had the trial, after I had been in prison, or maybe it was detention, I was released on that day, in the evening.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you had been convicted of the charges that were against you, how much jail time did you expect to receive?

utterances.speaker: Witness L-64
utterances.text: I don't know the laws, but I had consultations with my lawyer and I discussed with other people in jail and because of the arms dealing that I was accused of, it could be nine months or -- six months or nine months. This is what I thought, and I had served half of it because I had been in there for three and a half months.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After you were released from prison, were you and your family relocated outside of Kosovo? Please obviously do not say where.

utterances.speaker: Witness L-64
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After you were relocated outside of Kosovo, did you meet again with the Office of the Prosecutor at the end of 2003 and the beginning of 2004 and do an a witness statement concerning your time in Lapusnik?

utterances.speaker: Witness L-64
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you sign this statement on the 3rd of February, 2004?

utterances.speaker: Witness L-64
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you told us before that you joined the KLA in 1998. Can you tell us again what month you joined?

utterances.speaker: Witness L-64
utterances.text: It was shortly before the 9th of May. I was with a unit. After the 9th of May, I became a regular member.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's first talk about the time before the 9th of May. What was the unit that you were with?

utterances.speaker: Witness L-64
utterances.text: It was called the Zjarri unit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did that unit have a commander?

utterances.speaker: Witness L-64
utterances.text: Yes, it did. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who was the commander?

utterances.speaker: Witness L-64
utterances.text: The commander was Ymer Alushani.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned this person earlier in your evidence. How long had you known Ymer Alushani?

utterances.speaker: Witness L-64
utterances.text: I knew him from 1989. I mean the year 1989.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he have a pseudonym during the war?

utterances.speaker: Witness L-64
utterances.text: Yes, he did. His pseudonym was Voglushi.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What village was he from, if you know?

utterances.speaker: Witness L-64
utterances.text: Yes. He was born in the Komorane village where he also lived. In a neighbourhood in that village.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know which neighbourhood he lived in in Komorane?

utterances.speaker: Witness L-64
utterances.text: Yes. It was a neighbourhood that was not far from Lapusnik or the Lapusnik gorge.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us how you joined the Zjarri unit?

utterances.speaker: Witness L-64
utterances.text: Before the 9th of May we were collecting some weapons, war -- we could see that war had become inevitable and we were waiting only for it to start. I can't remember the exact date, but it was at the same time when Ymer had the licence, if I can say so, to create this unit. It was maybe a couple of months before the 9th of May, one or two months before that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, do you know how he got the licence to create the unit?

utterances.speaker: Witness L-64
utterances.text: I think - and that's what he said - he had contacts with some members in Likovc they were friends of his. And after he went to Likovc, he had the permission and the name of the unit. He had been also given some equipment, a couple of guns, two hand-grenades and so on. This was it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he tell you any of the names of the people who were in Likovc?

utterances.speaker: Witness L-64
utterances.text: I'm not very sure about the names. But numbers, he used numbers. He said number 25, and I think that that's the person he had contact -- he contacted first. Also he mentioned number 10, I think he mentioned Ilaz Kodra. But these were also mentioned regularly after that period, so -- so -- we know the names now but at that time we did not know the names.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Number 10, did you later learn the name of number 10?

utterances.speaker: Witness L-64
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what did you learn it to be?

utterances.speaker: Witness L-64
utterances.text: Rexhep Selimi.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you also mention number 25. Did you later learn the name of number 25?

utterances.speaker: Witness L-64
utterances.text: Yes, on the 9th of May. An incident had happened during the fighting, and I had given to number 25 a sniper rifle of Yugoslav make a couple of months ago. The fact was that I had lended it to him until I would need it again. I learned there that a person had been killed and this number 25 had rolled down -- had had an accident with a Jeep and the sniper rifle was damaged and then is when I learned -- at that time that I learned that his name was Ilaz Derguti.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when did you learn the name of number 10, Rexhep Selimi?

utterances.speaker: Witness L-64
utterances.text: I can't remember exactly, but it was during the fighting -- it was during the war, May, June, July, maybe even August. But I can't remember exactly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Aside from number 10 and number 25, did Ymer Alushani talk about any other names in connection with Likovc?

utterances.speaker: Witness L-64
utterances.text: Yes, he mentioned others.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember any of the others at this time?

utterances.speaker: Witness L-64
utterances.text: You mean before the 9th of May?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Did he -- do you remember him talking about any other people in connection with Likovc before the 9th of May, either by name or by pseudonym?

utterances.speaker: Witness L-64
utterances.text: I don't believe so. I can say maybe Muje Krasniqi, Ilaz Kodra. Ilaz was he was a friend of his. He was a close friend I think. He knew him from before. But I don't think he mentioned others.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Ymer Alushani tell you anything about Likovc, aside from the people who were there?

utterances.speaker: Witness L-64
utterances.text: No. Only when he went there he used to say, I'm going to the headquarters, to Likovc.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you yourself go to Likovc during this time, before the 9th of May?

utterances.speaker: Witness L-64
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you said that Ymer Alushani got some equipment, guns and grenades from Likovc. Do you remember when that was?

utterances.speaker: Witness L-64
utterances.text: He got those, I think maybe 20 days or at most, a month, before the 9th of May, two automatic rifle, two or three automatic rifles and -- and two boxes of hand-grenades.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know how many people were in this unit?

utterances.speaker: Witness L-64
utterances.text: There were 12 people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before the 9th of May, 1998, what did you and the others do in this unit?

utterances.speaker: Witness L-64
utterances.text: Well, in addition to getting prepared, sometimes we also used to escort somebody. On one occasion I escorted somebody to Orahovac. There was nothing major that we did. Once we tried to escort an inspector but it was impossible to get to Drenica, to Gllogovc. He was a Serbian -- well, he was an inspector of the Serbian service but he was Albanian.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what do you mean you tried to escort him?

utterances.speaker: Witness L-64
utterances.text: Well, we followed him. I mean we followed him. We wanted to kill him. And I know his name as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did anything happen? Did you try to kill him?

utterances.speaker: Witness L-64
utterances.text: We tried but it was impossible. We were spotted by other forces. There was a place Kroni i Mbretit close to the Koretica village so they spotted us and we could not go through with it. We left.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before the 9th of May did you and the others in the unit do anything else, engage in any other activities?

utterances.speaker: Witness L-64
utterances.text: Yes, we did. Yes. The Serbian forces were very aggressive at the time and at the smallest suspicion they opened fire immediately. And I know that several times, even when Ymer was not there, we responded to their fire, to the fire of the Serbian patrols. And on one occasion we went to someone and told him not to hang around with Serbs or Serbian secret service people. These kinds of things.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That one occasion that you went and told that person not to hang around with Serbs or Serbian secret service people, was that person an Albanian?

utterances.speaker: Witness L-64
utterances.text: Yes, Albanian.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you suspect that person of hanging around with Serbs or Serbian secret service people?

utterances.speaker: Witness L-64
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you recall what you said exactly to that person?

utterances.speaker: Witness L-64
utterances.text: That night we did not tell him anything. It was very late. We went to his yard, front yard. All of us were in uniform. I was a guard Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. at the entrance of the house, at the door. His family were concerned and many people came out, so they did not manage to tell him anything. They took two cars of the family, they told them that we need these two cars and he could go the next day to get them in Likovc. We thought that he would come to Likovc or would go to Likovc to get the cars and then we would tell him what we had to tell him, but at the house we did not tell him anything.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know if he went to Likovc?

utterances.speaker: Witness L-64
utterances.text: The next day he started to go to Likovc, but somewhere in Lapusnik he was stopped by someone who told him, It's better for you not to go to get the cars. If you are involved with the Serbian -- the Serbs, it's better for you not to go, so he did not go to Likovc. He did not get there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you have any further conversations with this person?

utterances.speaker: Witness L-64
utterances.text: No. After the war, he suspected that I was part -- I took part in taking his cars. He accused me of that, and we did not speak to each other. We haven't spoken to each other since.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You made reference to having a uniform. Where did you get the uniform?

utterances.speaker: Witness L-64
utterances.text: I only had -- it's not a uniform. It was a kind of a coat, overcoat, or a raincoat. But it was camouflage raincoat. But on that occasion, there were not only members of the Zjarri unit that went there, there were people from other units, and they had uniforms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: Witness L-64
utterances.text: And they brought uniforms for us that night.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who brought uniforms for you?

utterances.speaker: Witness L-64
utterances.text: The unit that came, some soldiers that came from Likovc, they had uniforms on. But they had also some reserves. For example, Ymer had a uniform himself. They had these raincoats. They were military raincoats and they gave them to us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In this period before the 9th of May, did you have a weapon?

utterances.speaker: Witness L-64
utterances.text: Yes, I always did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What kind of weapon was it?

utterances.speaker: Witness L-64
utterances.text: We had weapons at home. My grandfather did. I did have my own from 1991, 1992, they were automatic rifle, AK-47, Kalashnikovs. Two sniper rifles. And revolvers or pistols.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you have a particular speciality with regard to weapons?

utterances.speaker: Witness L-64
utterances.text: I know weapons well. I know them now, I have known them -- I knew them before, always known them.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I could just briefly go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Private.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in public.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We'll adjourn now for the first break and resume at five minutes past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, we are now back in public session, so I again remind to you take care not to mention your name or the names of any people in your family or anything that could identify you. And I want to start now with the topic of the 9th of May, 1998. Did something happen on that date?

utterances.speaker: Witness L-64
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened?

utterances.speaker: Witness L-64
utterances.text: On the 9th of May, it was after midday, two people came to my house, and they told me that Ymer wanted me to go to Lapusnik as fast as I could to get weapons, to some friends, some comrades, and go there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before those people came, did you know about anything happening in Lapusnik?

utterances.speaker: Witness L-64
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So what did you do?

utterances.speaker: Witness L-64
utterances.text: It was impossible for us at that moment to go by car through a territory where there were Serb police patrols, and I told my friends to leave later. So I told them to wait for us somewhere in the street. I told them the meeting place and we left before night came and we met with them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where did you go?

utterances.speaker: Witness L-64
utterances.text: We went to Komorane, to the house of Ymer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it night when you arrived at the house of Ymer?

utterances.speaker: Witness L-64
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Night had started to fall.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what did you find when you arrived at Ymer's house?

utterances.speaker: Witness L-64
utterances.text: There were other people there who had already come. The population was upset. Ymer wasn't there. We waited until he came, and he informed us of what had happened and he told to us leave that place after midnight; that is, we were supposed to go to Lapusnik before daylight.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did Ymer tell you had happened?

utterances.speaker: Witness L-64
utterances.text: He told us that the Serb police and army had attacked two villages in the vicinity of Lapusnik as well as in Lapusnik. They had fired against civilians in their homes. And upon hearing the fire shots, Ymer and come comrades had gone there and other units had come there in the meantime. Other units from other places. And there was fight going on until late in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Ymer -- and this is Ymer Alushani, is it not?

utterances.speaker: Witness L-64
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Ymer Alushani tell you anything about the other units that had come?

utterances.speaker: Witness L-64
utterances.text: Yes. He told us that units from Likovc had come to participate in the fighting. And that also a unit from Klecka had gone to Lapusnik to assist.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he tell you anything about the unit from Klecka?

utterances.speaker: Witness L-64
utterances.text: Yes. He told us that four or five people, I think, had come from Klecke with Celiku.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Ymer Alushani tell you anything about Celiku?

utterances.speaker: Witness L-64
utterances.text: No. He only said that Celiku had assisted the day in the fighting and that he had met with him. I think for the first time, yes, it was the first time that he met Celiku. And he told us how things had happened in Lapusnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he tell you anything about this meeting that he had with Celiku?

utterances.speaker: Witness L-64
utterances.text: No. There had been three other persons in Lapusnik before Ymer went there. And these soldiers from Klecke. And in the course of fighting, after the fighting broke out, they had withdrawn from their position. They had abandoned their position and they had suspicions about these persons. They had detained them taken away their weapons. Ymer said also that Celiku wanted to execute them, but that he had intervened and that he had allowed them to go home.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. I just have to try get a little clearer on this story. Who had withdrawn from their positions?

utterances.speaker: Witness L-64
utterances.text: Three soldiers who had been there. And they had introduced themselves as they were armed, and they had introduced themselves as members of LPK. They had withdrawn from their positions in the course of fighting, and they had stopped somewhere else. They wanted to leave the place to abandon -- to leave the population at their mercy.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did Ymer tell you where these three soldiers were from?

utterances.speaker: Witness L-64
utterances.text: Yes. The three of them were from Kishna Reka village. He told us that -- about one whom we both knew.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who was that?

utterances.speaker: Witness L-64
utterances.text: His name is Shaban Syla. He's from Kishna Reka village. Later I found out about the two others, because their family came to look for -- for them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you found out about the two others?

utterances.speaker: Witness L-64
utterances.text: I found out who they were. I don't know their names even now. I know their last name, I know they are from Kishna Reka.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: Witness L-64
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the last thing you said?

utterances.speaker: Witness L-64
utterances.text: They were two brothers. Two brothers, their last name was Kastrati and they were from Kishna Reka.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you said that Ymer told you that these three people had abandoned their positions and that other persons had detained them and taken away their weapons. Who detained them and took away their weapons, according to what Ymer told you?

utterances.speaker: Witness L-64
utterances.text: I told them that the soldiers who had come from Klecke with Celiku, they were the ones who stopped them, not Ymer. Ymer was a person who intervened for them not to have any problems, and so they were released, they were allowed to go home.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And just to be clear, this is something that you did not see yourself, but Ymer Alushani told you about this?

utterances.speaker: Witness L-64
utterances.text: I didn't see it myself. I wasn't there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could we go into closed session, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Closed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm sorry, private.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Private.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in public session.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, you testified that Ymer -- when you saw Ymer Alushani on the night of 9th of May that you told you to go to Lapusnik the following day. Did you do that?

utterances.speaker: Witness L-64
utterances.text: Yes. That night. But we left after midnight. That is, the night of the 9th of May, but we set out after midnight. It was at 2.00 in the morning, which means the 10th of May.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how did you go to Lapusnik? How did you get there?

utterances.speaker: Witness L-64
utterances.text: We went on foot.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did you go in Lapusnik?

utterances.speaker: Witness L-64
utterances.text: We went in the morning and took a natural position called Guri, or Big Guri, which is a stone, but there was a smaller one.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. The position that you took, Big Guri, where was that in relation to the Peja-Pristina road?

utterances.speaker: Witness L-64
utterances.text: It was on Peja-Pristina road on the right side. If you go from Pristina to Peja it's found on the left side, maybe 300, 400 metres away from the asphalt road.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And -- and what did you do when you got there?

utterances.speaker: Witness L-64
utterances.text: We waited until midday with the munitions and armaments we had. We divided -- gave them to some persons who had come to fight and didn't have weapons. It was at about midday, I think. In consultation with Ymer, together with another person, I went to the other part of Guri, where I could see from -- where I could see part of Komorane. We went there to see if there were some movements of troop, if some troops were coming from that direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Can we go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Private.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in public session.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Witness, you told us that consultation with Ymer you went to the other part of Guri from where you could see part of Komorane. What did you do there?

utterances.speaker: Witness L-64
utterances.text: Even though it was me, there was no greenery round. And this happened almost during all of the month of May. It was very cold. So we went to a place where we couldn't be seen from Komorane across checkpoint and from there we observed the movements of the police forces.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in the days -- did you stay there for -- in the days following the 10th of May?

utterances.speaker: Witness L-64
utterances.text: Yes, yes. We stayed there until the 26th of July.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in the days immediately following the 10th of May, aside from watching the movements of the police forces, did you do anything else?

utterances.speaker: Witness L-64
utterances.text: Yes. It was rain -- it was raining, and we had to put up a shelter, not to be seen by the Serb forces. We started to dig a trench. We did dug [as interpreted] a trench and then a hole which we enlarged later and transformed into a sort of bunker which was there until the end of the war. Every day we worked to build the position.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did this position later have a number?

utterances.speaker: Witness L-64
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was it?

utterances.speaker: Witness L-64
utterances.text: Until the 29 or the 30th of May, it was position number two, counting from the position -- from Guri. For a time, we called among ourselves position number one, because that was the first one to be led from Komorane. Later it became number two.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I think -- it was a little bit unclear. Was it first known as position one or first known as position number two?

utterances.speaker: Witness L-64
utterances.text: In the first days, since it was closer to Komorane, and the police cross checkpoint we call it position number one in the first days of May. But very soon this changed and the number started from Guri, being number one, and this being number two.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In those first days after the 10th of May, did you have any further discussions with Ymer Alushani?

utterances.speaker: Witness L-64
utterances.text: Yes, we talked every day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what did you talk about in those first few days?

utterances.speaker: Witness L-64
utterances.text: We talked mainly about weapons, what -- about what we were going to do, how to become stronger, and these things. We discussed that we had to stay in the trenches, in the positions during all the time and to move only at night, not to be seen.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have any discussions during these first few days about Celiku?

utterances.speaker: Witness L-64
utterances.text: No. Until the 12th of May, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there any fighting during these days from the 10th of May on? Was there any further fighting with the Serb forces?

utterances.speaker: Witness L-64
utterances.text: No. There wasn't, until the 29th of May. There was some shelling, sporadic shelling, but there was no attack.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A few days after the 9th of May was there a meeting in Lapusnik?

utterances.speaker: Witness L-64
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where was the meeting?

utterances.speaker: Witness L-64
utterances.text: In in the evening or at night we were sleeping in some houses close to the Guri position. In the evening two or three people had come, and all the soldiers had gathered together. I went there later, together two other comrades and Fehmi Lladrovci had come. Somebody said that Celiku is here, but I can't remember and I did not know him at the time whether he was there or not. Fehmi spoke about the war about half an hour, how the war would be conducted and so on, and in the end he said Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. that, We will all be fighting together, together with a Klecka unit, in the Klecka unit. Celiku unit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was Ymer Alushani there?

utterances.speaker: Witness L-64
utterances.text: Yes, he was there. And we all wrote down our names in a notebook. And we gave that notebook to Fehmi Lladrovci. He took it with himself. We signed it as well. And he told us not to be concerned about our families because we would be -- our families would have assistance and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This notebook that you wrote your name in and you signed, what did you think that meant?

utterances.speaker: Witness L-64
utterances.text: That meant that -- how many people we were in that position, who these people were. These were notes that were taken regularly after that period. So the notebook contains the names, surnames, dates of birth, and -- from -- the place from where we came from and also our signatures.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was this information taken in connection with the fact that you had now been made part of the Celiku unit?

utterances.speaker: Witness L-64
utterances.text: Yes. After a moment we became part of the Celiku unit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you given a number?

utterances.speaker: Witness L-64
utterances.text: No, there were no numbers at the moment. What do you mean, numbers? We were not given numbers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In connection with being -- becoming part of the Celiku unit, was your unit given any particular number?

utterances.speaker: Witness L-64
utterances.text: Not on that day, no. I have seen it somewhere that we were told that it was Celiku 3, but it was not on that day. Maybe I've said it, but I was not thinking right. But it was not on that day, I'm sure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it a later day that you became Celiku 3?

utterances.speaker: Witness L-64
utterances.text: Yes. Maybe two or three days later. Not on that day. It was soon after though.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'll ask you about that in a moment. But first could tell us -- you mentioned this person Fehmi Lladrovci. Did you know who that person was?

utterances.speaker: Witness L-64
utterances.text: No. That's where I got to know him, at that place. But he spoke to us about his biography that he had been a fighter in Croatia. After Croatia he had gone somewhere, to a western country, and then he had come back to Kosovo together with his wife to fight. He was a tall man. We were very happy to see him because he looked a very brave man, very determined.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did anything else happen at this meeting that you have described?

utterances.speaker: Witness L-64
utterances.text: No. After Fehmi Lladrovci left, together with some other people, many questions were asked of Ymer. Ymer -- we asked Ymer, How is this possible, what will become of our unit? Maybe Ymer had spoken to somebody else and he did not give any explanations. He just said that, We are here to fight, and it's not important who we fight with. The important thing is to fight.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did he say anything else?

utterances.speaker: Witness L-64
utterances.text: I can't remember that he did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you have already referred to something that occurred a few days later. Was there another meeting a few days later?

utterances.speaker: Witness L-64
utterances.text: I can't remember exactly how many days, two or three after that, but it was in the afternoon. We all gathered together on an open place. Some people came from Klecka. That's where we got to know Celiku. He spoke to us. We were lined up, and after he held his speech he said that, From now on, you will have our help. We will get stronger and we will fight, and from today the Lapusnik position will be called Celiku 3. And the decision about the commander, not a commander because there was no commander at that time. It was more of a person responsible for the position. That would be Qerqizi and he said that, Anything you have you must discuss with him, any need you might have you go to him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Celiku say anything about what his position was?

utterances.speaker: Witness L-64
utterances.text: No. He only said that, I am responsible for this territory and you -- up to Klecka, and anything you have you can do it through Qerqizi. You tell Qerqizi.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that Qerqiz would be the "person responsible for the position." To be clear, what position is that?

utterances.speaker: Witness L-64
utterances.text: The Lapusnik position. That is how it would be decided, that Qerqizi would be responsible. And Qerqizi would be the one that would communicate with Celiku for anything that was necessary.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was Qerqizi at this meeting?

utterances.speaker: Witness L-64
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, he was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he say anything?

utterances.speaker: Witness L-64
utterances.text: No, nothing. Not on that day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Celiku say how matters would be communicated from Qerqizi to him, how the communication would occur?

utterances.speaker: Witness L-64
utterances.text: I said that -- that anything would -- we would need, any question, anything, we would address that to Qerqizi and then he would convey those things to Celiku.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did he say anything about how Qerqizi would communicate with Celiku, how he would actually have that communication?

utterances.speaker: Witness L-64
utterances.text: No. No, he did not say anything.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that before Celiku made this announcement that he made a speech. Do you remember what he said in his speech?

utterances.speaker: Witness L-64
utterances.text: I remember approximately. Things like we have to be disciplined; we all know why we are here, our purpose. We have to defend or positions to our death. The Serbian forces can only step on our bodies to get to the civilian population. This is more or less what he said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Approximately how many soldiers were there for this meeting?

utterances.speaker: Witness L-64
utterances.text: About 20 soldiers. Because soldiers used to come every day. There were over 20 or about 20 soldiers. The number had increased. Many others had come. People used to come every day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know Celiku's real name at this time?

utterances.speaker: Witness L-64
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you learn his real name later?

utterances.speaker: Witness L-64
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did you learn it, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: Witness L-64
utterances.text: I think it was June. From a person who was with us. His pseudonym was Vetura, and he said that he was his uncle. He was from Banja, the Banja village and told us his name.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what name did he tell you?

utterances.speaker: Witness L-64
utterances.text: Fatmir Limaj.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This person Qerqiz, did you know his real name on that day?

utterances.speaker: Witness L-64
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you learn his real name later?

utterances.speaker: Witness L-64
utterances.text: Yes. Maybe in August or September. Much later, but not in Lapusnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you learn his real name to be?

utterances.speaker: Witness L-64
utterances.text: His name was Isak. But I didn't know his surname until after the war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you learn his surname to be after the war?

utterances.speaker: Witness L-64
utterances.text: After the war, I learned that his name was Isak Musliu. I knew where he was from. I had met him once in Ferizaj.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did you learn him to be from?

utterances.speaker: Witness L-64
utterances.text: A village close to Shtime.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know the name of the village?

utterances.speaker: Witness L-64
utterances.text: There were many soldiers from these two villages. It could be either Recak or Petrove, but I think it -- mostly that it is Recak.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember when after the war you learned his real name?

utterances.speaker: Witness L-64
utterances.text: It was immediately after the war, or soon after the war. In 1999. I can't remember exactly when.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you've testified that on -- at this meeting Celiku said that Qerqiz would be the person responsible for the position at Lapusnik. Did that in fact happen, was he then the person responsible for the position at Lapusnik?

utterances.speaker: Witness L-64
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, he was. Although there was -- there were some polemics with Ymer about the change of name and command. But things were clarified. It was the same, all the same to us, because our purpose was to be there to fight.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long did he stay in that position as the person responsible for the position at Lapusnik? Qerqiz, that is. Until what date?

utterances.speaker: Witness L-64
utterances.text: Until it existed. Until the formation existed. Until the 26th of July, 1998.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And during that time was Celiku the person above him in command or responsible -- in responsibility?

utterances.speaker: Witness L-64
utterances.text: Yes. The number of the units and the volunteers increased daily. And Celiku was responsible for Qerqiz and for us all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And during these months, from the time of this meeting in May, through June and July, where was Celiku based?

utterances.speaker: Witness L-64
utterances.text: The base was at Klecka. It is a village on the hills in Berisa. It is on the top of the hills, and it is called Klecke. There's where his base was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And during that time, during the rest of May, June and July, was the position at Lapusnik known as Celiku 3?

utterances.speaker: Witness L-64
utterances.text: Yes, all the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you said there were some polemics with Ymer Alushani. Can you explain a little bit about that? What did you mean about that?

utterances.speaker: Witness L-64
utterances.text: There was a kind of dissatisfaction expressed by some people there. Because people knew Ymer, knew about his skills and many people came there because of Ymer, because Ymer was skilled. He was able in war affairs. Maybe not polemics, but there was some disagreement and people went to Ymer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what did Ymer say, if you know?

utterances.speaker: Witness L-64
utterances.text: Well, he looked dissatisfied but he did not express that. He did not say anything himself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what position, if any, did Ymer have during this time period, during the rest of May, June and July?

utterances.speaker: Witness L-64
utterances.text: There were -- there was no special way to call him, except his pseudonym. But he was always with Qerqizi, close to him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he respect Qerqiz as the person responsible for the position at Lapusnik?

utterances.speaker: Witness L-64
utterances.text: Yes. And he loved him very much.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you said there was some dissatisfaction expressed by people. Did this result in anything? Did anything happen as a result of this dissatisfaction?

utterances.speaker: Witness L-64
utterances.text: No, nothing. This happened only early in time. And this was the dissatisfaction of people who were with Ymer at the time. But nothing happened. This was something we discussed with Ymer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you aware of anybody in -- any soldiers in Lapusnik who refused to recognise Qerqiz as the person responsible for the position?

utterances.speaker: Witness L-64
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned earlier that the next occasion when there was fighting was on the 29th of May, 1998. Can you tell us what happened on that date?

utterances.speaker: Witness L-64
utterances.text: Yes. Briefly, early in the morning there were many Serb forces at the Komorane crossroads, tanks, APCs, and before they even attacked they started shelling our positions with grenade launchers from the Quka e Komoranit, from the Komorane crossroads. There was a military base as well there, but it was some metres further down from the crossroads. And this happened during all that day, until the late hours in the afternoon. There was shelling until 10.00 p.m., I think. From the distance.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you yourself participate in the fighting?

utterances.speaker: Witness L-64
utterances.text: Yes. And I think I was the first to shoot a round.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where were you when you were fighting?

utterances.speaker: Witness L-64
utterances.text: I was at my position, where we had worked. It was point 2, and we -- there was this field in front of us, and there was this infantry unit coming towards us. It had created a kind of arrow shape, this unit. This position was the only one that was grouped there in Lapusnik. When I saw them, I asked Qerqizi, Where can I shoot? And he said, On the first one. And I think I hit the first one. Very soon all the others fell to the ground and rolled on the ground. I started shooting again. I don't know if I hit anybody after that. The APCs were coming closer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what happened as a result of this fight? Or let me put it a different way: What was the result of the fighting on that day?

utterances.speaker: Witness L-64
utterances.text: The result was that the Serb forces and the army could not penetrate to our positions that we had at the time, but we were helped by other positions because people were fighting from the opposite site of the asphalt road as well. Many civilians, armed civilians came to help us and they positioned themselves on the hills and were fighting. Around midday, a unit came from Lladroc, a unit of 20 strong, 50 or 20 strong. They were commanded by a person. He was a military man. He looked like one. He had been an officer in the Yugoslavia army, I learned later. And I had to intervene to stop them because they wanted to go out there in front of the Serb forces so I had to stop them. Some of them went to the position at the guri. Three or four of them came to the position where I was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know the name of the person that commended this unit from Lladroc?

utterances.speaker: Witness L-64
utterances.text: Yes, he was from the village of Kishna Reka and his name was Ejet [phoen] Kastrati. I learned his name on that day from his soldiers. Later they contributed, he contributed opening trenches and positions in Lapusnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was Celiku present for the fighting on this day, on the 29th of May?

utterances.speaker: Witness L-64
utterances.text: Three people came together with Celiku around 10.00 or 11.00. It was after 9.00. 10.00 or 11.00. One of the others was Kumanova. There was a sniper with Kumanova. He stayed at the position, position 2, for some time. And enemy tank was stuck in the mud and could not get out. Celiku took a mortar from one of the soldiers and asked, Who knows the terrain on the other side? So he went with a person, the other person, I believe he was a civilian. He tried to -- to fire at the tank, but it was impossible because there was coverage so the tank was covered by fire from the enemy. So he came back to our position without having fired the tank -- on the tank.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You made a reference to a person known as Kumanova. Did you know on that day who that person was?

utterances.speaker: Witness L-64
utterances.text: I had heard about him before, but it was the first time I saw him. He was wounded in his legs. He had been wounded earlier, so he had difficulty in walking.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say he had been wounded earlier, you mean before the 29th of May?

utterances.speaker: Witness L-64
utterances.text: Yes, before the 29th of May. They had met an ambush, a Serbian police ambush, and -- I don't know when, but it was before the 29th of May.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the 29th of May, did you know this person's real name?

utterances.speaker: Witness L-64
utterances.text: Of Kumanova, you mean?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, of Kumanova.

utterances.speaker: Witness L-64
utterances.text: No. No, I only knew him as Kumanova.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you learn his real name later?

utterances.speaker: Witness L-64
utterances.text: Yes. I learned that he was from Kumanova, which is in Macedonia, that he had come from the west to fight in Kosova. He was very brave. That is all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But what did you learn his real name to be later?

utterances.speaker: Witness L-64
utterances.text: It was Ismet Jashari.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And on the 29th of May, did you know -- had you heard anything about what his position was?

utterances.speaker: Witness L-64
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, I'm going to show you a book that -- that you provided to the OTP with the assistance of the usher. And this is --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: It's at tab 12. There is an Albanian -- there's a copy of the Albanian, which is copy of the original book. And there is an English translation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, can you tell us what that book is?

utterances.speaker: Witness L-64
utterances.text: This is a notebook. I have written down some notes on it. During the war, I kept notes, not in this book normally. It was in a smaller notebook or loose sheets of paper and after that I wrote them down here. Many of the things that I wrote here I copied them down from my notes after the war. I thought that it would be important to keep such notes about the war. So these are part of my notes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And does the notebook cover different parts of the war, different time periods of the war?

utterances.speaker: Witness L-64
utterances.text: Yes. And different time periods, other periods, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are the entries in the book written in order, in time order?

utterances.speaker: Witness L-64
utterances.text: Approximately, yes. But some of the things have been written towards the end of the book. Because I did not know where to put them, these notes, and I wrote them -- that's why I wrote them towards the end of the book. Some of my notes had been damaged during the war, so I wrote them down where I could.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me draw your attention to some specific parts of the book and ask you if you could turn --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And maybe if the usher could assist the witness on this. To page U003-6994, on the English translation that is page 8.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Witness, in this section -- Yes, I have been asked to give the ERN number again. In the Albanian it's U003-6994 to page U003-7003. Now, Witness, in that section there are some entries that are dated 12 May, 1998; 14 May, 1998; 21 May, 1998 and 29 May of 1998. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: Witness L-64
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us when you wrote those entries in that book?

utterances.speaker: Witness L-64
utterances.text: These were notes that I took in another notebook but they -- these notes were taken at the time, in May. But maybe I copied them down here in August or September. It's at that time that I started to write on this notebook. Maybe these notes were not taken on the same day but the next day, or sometimes in the evening. Sometimes I used to take notes two or three days later, to write the notes down two or three days later.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you say that you think you may have written them in that book in August or September, that's August or September of what year?

utterances.speaker: Witness L-64
utterances.text: August, September 1998. As I said, I had taken down these notes at that time in May, but I copied them to this notebook in August or September.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, if you would look at the entry for the 12th of May, 1998. It's halfway down on 6994. Do you see that, the entry for the 12th of May?

utterances.speaker: Witness L-64
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you just read that --

utterances.speaker: Witness L-64
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you just read that, what is enter the there for the 12th of May.

utterances.speaker: Witness L-64
utterances.text: From the beginning?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, just what is on the 12th of May. It's about halfway down on 6994, 12 May, 1998.

utterances.speaker: Witness L-64
utterances.text: "The day went by without any fighting. We were preparing ourselves and getting stronger every day.
